The second step is to cleave the propane and 2 produce three moles of free fatty acids (Pearlson 2011) per mole of triglycerides. The glycerol portion of the triglyceride molecule is converted into propane by adding H . The third reaction is 2 to remove the oxygen from the fatty acids (Pearlson 2011). There are three pathways occurring in this stage: decarboxylation, decarbonylation, and hydrodeoxygenation. The decarboxylation pathway removes oxygen in the form of CO , decarbonylation removes oxygen in the form of 2 carbon monoxide (CO), and hydrodeoxygenation removes oxygen in the form of H O. 2 Hydrogenation takes place to saturate the double bonds in the unsaturated triglycerides. The hydroisomerization and hydrocracking processes are followed by a fractionation process to separate the mixtures into paraffinic kerosene, paraffinic diesel, naphtha, and light gases. The hydrocracking reaction is exothermic and results in the production of lighter liquid and gas products. They are relatively slow reactions; thus, most of the hydrocracking takes place in the last section of the reactor. The hydrocracking reactions primarily involve cracking and saturation of paraffins. This pathway is based on the models developed previously (Tao, Milbrandt, et al. 2017), with all values reported in $2023. Yellow Grease. Yellow grease could be processed via the HEFA pathway to produce HC. Feedstock cost is assumed to be $550/ton ($0.61/kg) (Milbrandt and Badgett 2024). Availability of yellow grease varies significantly between 50 and 100 miles near BAF, and both have small volumes to support a biorefinery facility converting yellow grease using the HEFA pathway concept. Assuming a yellow grease price of $0.61/kg, the MFSP of the hydrocarbon (HC) via the HEFA-SPK pathway is estimated at approximately $6.40/gge (Table 9) for 50 miles and $4.49/gge for feedstocks from a 100-mile collection radius. This means that HC could be more than twice as expensive as compared to conventional jet fuel with yellow grease. The conversion cost without considering feedstock cost would be about $3.9–$2.0/gge. Annual HC production is estimated to be 3.0–15.9 million gge (MMgge). Yellow grease alone is not a viable option as a HC feedstock due to its high feedstock cost and limited availability within 50–100 miles of BAF. Yellow grease and other FOGs have a relatively high selling price due to commoditization for bio-oils and other industries. Select FOG sources may have resources to offset costs, as well as benefiting from economies of scale, typically in areas with organic waste disposal bans, high population densities, and high landfill tipping fees. It is recommended to take advantage of these programs if they are available within 50–100 miles of BAF.
